In [[applied statistics]], (e.g., applied to the [[social science]]s and [[psychometrics]]), '''common-method variance'''  ('''CMV''') is the spurious "variance that is attributable to the [[measurement]] method rather than to the [[construct (philosophy of science)|constructs]] the measures are assumed to represent"<ref name="podsakoff2003">{{cite journal |last1=Podsakoff |first1=P.M. |last2=MacKenzie |first2=S.B. |last3=Lee |first3=J.-Y. |last4=Podsakoff |first4=N.P. |title=Common method biases in behavioral research: A critical review of the literature and recommended remedies |journal=Journal of Applied Psychology |volume=88 |issue=5 |pages=879–903 |date=October 2003 |doi=10.1037/0021-9010.88.5.879 |url=http://www.personal.psu.edu/jxb14/M554/articles/Podsakoffetal2003.pdf |pmid=14516251|hdl=2027.42/147112 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> or equivalently as "systematic error variance shared among variables measured with and introduced as a function of the same method and/or source".<ref name="richardson2009">{{cite journal |last1=Richardson |first1=H.A. |last2=Simmering |first2=M.J. |last3=Sturman |first3=M.C. |title=A tale of three perspectives: Examining post hoc statistical techniques for detection and correction of common method variance |journal=Organizational Research Methods |volume=12 |issue=4 |pages=762–800 |date=October 2009 |doi=10.1177/1094428109332834 |hdl=1813/72364 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> For example, an electronic survey method might influence results for those who might be unfamiliar with an electronic survey interface differently than for those who might be familiar. If measures are affected by CMV or '''common-method bias''', the intercorrelations among them can be inflated or deflated depending upon several factors.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Williams | first1 = L. J. | last2 = Brown | first2 = B. K. | year = 1994 | title = Method variance in organizational behavior and human resources research: Effects on correlations, path coefficients, and hypothesis testing | journal = Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes | volume = 57 | issue = 2| pages = 185–209 | doi=10.1006/obhd.1994.1011}}</ref> Although it is sometimes assumed that CMV affects all variables, evidence suggests that whether or not the correlation between two variables is affected by CMV is a function of both the method and the particular constructs being measured.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Spector | first1 = P. E. | year = 2006 | title = Method Variance in Organizational Research: Truth or Urban Legend? | journal = Organizational Research Methods | volume = 9 | issue = 2| pages = 221–232 | doi = 10.1177/1094428105284955 }}</ref><!-- ==Sources== c.f. podsakoff2003 -->

==Remedies==

===Ex ante remedies===

Several [[ex ante]] remedies exist that help to avoid or minimize possible common method variance. Important remedies have been compiled and discussed by Chang et al. (2010), Lindell & Whitney (2001) and Podsakoff et al. (2003).<ref name="chang2010">{{cite journal |last1=Chang |first1=S.-J. |last2=van Witteloostuijn |first2=A. |last3=Eden |first3=L. |title=Common method variance in international business research |journal=Journal of International Business Studies |volume=41 |pages=178–184 |year=2010 |doi=10.1057/jibs.2009.88 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="lindell2001">{{cite journal | last1=Lindell |first1=M. K. | last2=Whitney | first2=D. J. |year=2001 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12032562 | title=Accounting for common method variance in cross-sectional research designs. | journal=Journal of Applied Psychology | volume=86 | issue=1 | pages=114–121 | doi=10.1037/0021-9010.86.1.114|pmid=11302223 }}</ref><ref name="podsakoff2003" />

===Ex post remedies===

Using simulated data sets, Richardson et al. (2009) investigate three [[ex post]] techniques to test for common method variance: the correlational marker technique, the [[confirmatory factor analysis]] (CFA) marker technique, and the unmeasured latent method construct (ULMC) technique. Only the CFA marker technique turns out to provide some value, whereas the commonly used Harman test does not turn out to provide such value.<ref name="richardson2009"/> A comprehensive example of this technique has been demonstrated by Williams et al. (2010).<ref name="williams2010">{{cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=L.J. |last2=Hartman |first2=N. |last3=Cavazotte |first3=F. |title=Method variance and marker variables: A review and comprehensive CFA marker technique |journal=Organizational Research Methods |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=477–514 |date=July 2010 |doi=10.1177/1094428110366036 }}</ref> Kock (2015) discusses a full collinearity test that is successful in the identification of common method bias with a model that nevertheless passes standard convergent and discriminant validity assessment criteria based on a CFA.<ref>Kock, N. (2015). [https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B76EXfrQqs3hYlZhTWdWcXRockU/view Common method bias in PLS-SEM: A full collinearity assessment approach.] International Journal of e-Collaboration, 11(4), 1-10.</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kock |first1=N. |last2=Lynn |first2=G. S. |year=2012 |url=http://www.scriptwarp.com/warppls/pubs/Kock_Lynn_2012.pdf |title=Lateral collinearity and misleading results in variance-based SEM: An illustration and recommendations |journal=Journal of the Association for Information Systems |volume=13 |issue=7 |pages=546&ndash;580 |doi=10.17705/1jais.00302 }}</ref>
